Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of the same problem, until the problem becomes so simple it can be answered directly. That "simple enough to answer directly" case is called the **base case**, and every recursive function needs one — without it, the function would call itself forever. Each call to the function adds a new layer on top of the previous ones, like stacking plates, and when the base case is finally reached, the answers start bubbling back up through the layers until the original call gets its result. A classic example is `factorial(n)`: if `n` is 0, return 1 (the base case); otherwise, return `n * factorial(n - 1)`, which keeps multiplying by the next smaller factorial until it hits 0.
